# Sivijātaka (Ja 499)

**ID:** Ja 499
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Sivijātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Prince Sivi
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja499
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul14.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sivijātaka* (Ja 499), translated as *Prince Sivi*, is one of the most prominent bodily gift (*dehadāna*) stories in Pali Buddhist literature [Wood 2005; SuttaCentral]. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the story at Jetavana regarding the "incomparable gift" (*asadisadāna*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1897]. In the narrative past, the Bodhisatta was King Sivi, a ruler renowned for boundless generosity who resolved to make an unprecedented "internal" bodily sacrifice (*ajjhattikadāna*) [Ohnuma 2007; Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh, and Blood]. When the god Sakka tests his virtue by appearing as a blind brahmin demanding eyes, King Sivi joyfully resolves to give them, comparing their extraction to pulling the pith out of a palm tree (*tālamiñja*) [Ohnuma 2007; Chen 2015]. Despite grief among his subjects and the reluctance of the surgeon Sīvaka, the eyes are detached and transferred to the supplicant [Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh, and Blood; Ohnuma, Dissertation]. Encouraged by Sakka, the blinded king subsequently makes an Act of Truth (*saccakiriya*), miraculously restoring his eyesight before renouncing worldly kingship to live as an ascetic in the royal park [Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh, and Blood; Ohnuma, Dissertation].

From a metrical and philological perspective, K. R. Norman observes that the verses of the *Sivijātaka* consist of a mixture of archaic Triṣṭubh/Jagatī metres and later Anuṣṭubh (Śloka) metres [Norman 1983]. Text-critical analysis shows that isolating and removing the secondary Anuṣṭubh verses leaves an older metrical narrative poem that is complete in itself [Norman 1983].

In terms of parallels and text reuse, a condensed, versified first-person account of the episode is found in the *Sivirājacariyam* of the *Cariyāpiṭaka* [Ohnuma, Dissertation]. SuttaCentral identifies passage-level parallels in the *Apadāna* (Tha-Ap 59 and Tha-Ap 418) and references in the *Vimānavatthu* (Vv 83) and *Petavatthu* (Pv 17) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus indicates extensive internal Pali reuse with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (4,758 characters) and the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* (3,143 characters) [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, DharmaNexus automatically aligns the text with Sanskrit and Tibetan versions of Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā* (Tibetan D4150; Sanskrit with a match score of 75), the *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra*, and the *Dānaparikathā* [DharmaNexus]. Scholars note that whereas other Buddhist traditions frequently transmit two distinct Śibi narratives—one where he gives flesh to save a dove from a hawk, and another where he gives his eyes—the Pali *Sivijātaka* explicitly preserves the gift of the eyes [Murphy; Chandawimala].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Passage-level parallels (SuttaCentral): Tha-Ap 59 Pañcadīpakattheraapadāna
- Resembling parallels (SuttaCentral): Tha-Ap 418 Ekadīpiyattheraapadāna
- Mentioned in (SuttaCentral): Vv 83 Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvimānavatthu; Pv 17 Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīpetavatthu
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§2.4–6.4 ↔ §4054–4064); Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0512a) (§2.1–6.4 ↔ §479–491)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): སྐྱེས་པའི་རབས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད། (jātakamāla) (D4150) [bo]; Āryaśūra: Jātakamālā (SA_T09_ajm_u) [sa]; འཕགས་པ་སྙིང་རྗེ་པད་མ་དཀར་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་མདོ། (ārya-karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra) (D0112) [bo]; སྦྱིན་པའི་གཏམ། (dānaparikathā) (D4161) [bo]; ཐབས་མཁས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་དྲིན་ལན་བསབ་པའི་མདོ། (D0353) [bo]; 央掘魔羅經 (ZH_T02_0120) [zh]

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja499 — Supplied the canonical metadata, English title, framing story summary, and Apadāna/Vimānavatthu/Petavatthu parallels.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text-reuse database for ja499 — Provided text-reuse alignments with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā, Āryaśūra's Jātakamālā, Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra, and Dānaparikathā.
- [Wood 2005] Leela Aditi Wood, Buddha and the Shape of Belief: Indic Visual Jatakamalas, vol. 1 (2005) — Discussed the Sivi Jātaka as a central narrative of bodily self-sacrifice (dehadāna).
- [Murphy] Stephen A. Murphy, Buddhist Boundary Markers of Northeast Thailand and Central Laos, 7th-12th C…Khorat Plateau — Noted the differentiation of the Pali Sivi Jātaka giving eyes versus the Sanskrit/avadāna flesh-and-dove tale.
- [Ohnuma 2007] Reiko Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh and Blood: Giving Away the Body in Indian Buddhist Literature (2007) — Analyzed King Sivi's unprecedented gift, Sakka's testing, and the palm tree pith (tālamiñja) simile.
- [Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh, and Blood] Reiko Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh, and Blood: The Body in Buddhist Literature — Documented the reluctant surgeon Sīvaka, the classification of internal gifts, and the Act of Truth restoring the king's eyes.
- [Ohnuma, Dissertation] Reiko Ohnuma, Dehadāna: The Gift of the Body in Indian Buddhist Narrative Literature (Ph.D. dissertation) — Provided textual details on the surgical extraction, the king's retirement to the royal park, and the Cariyāpiṭaka parallel (Sivirājacariyam).
- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pali Literature: Including the Canonical Literature in Prakrit and Sanskrit of all the Hīnayāna Schools of Buddhism (1983) — Described the metrical composition of Ja 499, distinguishing older Triṣṭubh/Jagatī from later Anuṣṭubh verses.
- [Chen 2015] Lang Chen, Heroic Sinners: Evil in Buddhist Narrative Literature (2015) — Discussed the role of Sakka as a tester of the Bodhisattva's virtue in the Sivi Jātaka.
- [Chandawimala] Rangama Chandawimala Thero, Impact of the Abhayagiri Practices on Development of Theravada Buddhism in Sri Lanka — Noted the textual bifurcation between King Sibi's parting with his eyes and the dove/flesh narrative.
- [Fausböll 1897] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 7 (1897) — Confirmed the reference to the Sovīrajātaka and the introductory asadisadāna motif in connection with Ja 499.
- [Jory 2016] Patrick Jory, Thailand's Theory of Monarchy: Vessantara Jātaka and the Idea of the Perfect Man (2016) — Noted the place of King Sivi's eye-donation in vernacular Southeast Asian transmissions of the perfections.
